Tensor completion, injectivity and state domination

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra, September 2026. New original text: public domain (CC0).

A completed tensor has two descriptions here: a Cauchy sequence for the projective norm π\piπ, and a Cauchy sequence for the symmetric norm σ\sigmaσ. Because σ≤π\sigma\le\piσ≤π, the algebraic identity gives a map from the first completion to the second. The random lift construction supplies a projective preimage of every self-adjoint target vector, with cost at most (81/16)∥v∥σ+ε(81/16)\|v\|_\sigma+\varepsilon(81/16)∥v∥σ​+ε. Different choices of ε\varepsilonε could still give different preimages. Their difference lies in the kernel of the completion map.

We prove that this kernel is zero. A normalized functional detects a kernel vector only through its real part; the bilinear exponential test makes that real part σ\sigmaσ-continuous. A Gaussian then turns the resulting two numerical-reality conditions into a norm bound tending to zero. Once the lift is unique, its approximate costs become an exact norm comparison. That comparison makes every bounded real bilinear form eligible for the final compact affine argument, which chooses one pair of states for all inputs.

The two algebraic tensor norms are

∥u∥π=inf⁡u=∑jxj⊗yj∑j∥xj∥∥yj∥,∥u∥σ=inf⁡u=∑jxj⊗yj∥∑jq(xj)∥1/2∥∑jq(yj)∥1/2.\|u\|_\pi=\inf_{u=\sum_jx_j\otimes y_j}\sum_j\|x_j\|\|y_j\|, \qquad \|u\|_\sigma=\inf_{u=\sum_jx_j\otimes y_j} \Big\|\sum_jq(x_j)\Big\|^{1/2}\Big\|\sum_jq(y_j)\Big\|^{1/2}.∥u∥π​=u=∑j​xj​⊗yj​inf​j∑​∥xj​∥∥yj​∥,∥u∥σ​=u=∑j​xj​⊗yj​inf​​j∑​q(xj​)​1/2​j∑​q(yj​)​1/2.

Both infima use finite decompositions. The real projective norm uses self-adjoint factors and real scalars. A bounded form acts on these completions when its value on an algebraic tensor is bounded by the corresponding norm; its dual norm is the least such bound.

Section 8.1 proves real and complex functional extension. Section 8.2 constructs the completion maps and the projective algebra. Section 8.3 constructs the states, using the scalar spectrum, continuous calculus and order proved in ITP F01–F13. The scalar foundations and continuous norm integrals are in Elementary calculus for infinite products. Section 9 proves compactness and convergent subnets for arbitrary dual balls. None of these constructions assumes separability. A unital algebra in the state assertions has a nonzero identity of norm one; the injectivity assertion also includes zero and nonunital algebras.

From small lifts to the real tensor bound

The kernel theorem makes a small preimage unique. Before transferring its cost, we identify the real completion inside the complex one. The real projective space embeds in the complex projective space. To see this without assuming a tensor-inclusion theorem, expand any complex decomposition of a self-adjoint tensor as in (6) of the preceding lesson. It costs at most twice the original projective cost, since ∥Re⁡x∥2+∥Im⁡x∥2≤2∥x∥2\|\operatorname{Re}x\|^2+\|\operatorname{Im}x\|^2\le2\|x\|^2∥Rex∥2+∥Imx∥2≤2∥x∥2. Thus

on the algebraic real tensor space, and the inclusion of its completion is injective. Its image is the self-adjoint part of the complex completion: symmetrized algebraic approximants are Cauchy by (8).

7. Exercises with complete solutions

The first three checks build the functional that tests a kernel vector. Exercises 4–6 examine the compactness and Gaussian estimates that make the test decisive. Exercises 7–8 transfer a completed lift's cost. Exercises 9–10 turn those norm estimates into common-state bounds.

Exercise 1. Let VVV be the normalized bilinear form used in Lemma 1.1, with marginal states φ,ψ\varphi,\psiφ,ψ, and let a,ba,ba,b be self-adjoint. Test VVV on (eita,eitb)(e^{ita},e^{itb})(eita,eitb). ∣R(t)∣≤M3eM6∣t∣3.|R(t)|\le \frac{M^3e^M}{6}|t|^3.∣R(t)∣≤6M3eM​∣t∣3.

Both exponentials have norm one, so their bilinear value has real part at most one. Subtract one and divide by t2>0t^2>0t2>0:

−B+Re⁡R(t)t2≤0.-B+\frac{\operatorname{Re}R(t)}{t^2}\le0.−B+t2ReR(t)​≤0.

The last quotient tends to zero, proving B≥0B\ge0B≥0. Thus Re⁡V(a,b)≥−[φ(a2)+ψ(b2)]/2\operatorname{Re}V(a,b)\ge-[\varphi(a^2)+\psi(b^2)]/2ReV(a,b)≥−[φ(a2)+ψ(b2)]/2. Exercise 3. A kernel vector is tested by the self-adjoint part of a normalized functional. Let CCC be an involutive complex Banach algebra whose involution is isometric and whose identity has norm one. If F∈SCF\in\mathcal S_CF∈SC​, verify that

The involution carries the unit ball onto itself. Substituting z=x∗z=x^*z=x∗ in the functional norm supremum therefore gives ∥F∗∥=sup⁡∥z∥≤1∣F(z)∣=∥F∥=1\|F^*\|=\sup_{\|z\|\le1}|F(z)|=\|F\|=1∥F∗∥=sup∥z∥≤1​∣F(z)∣=∥F∥=1. The triangle inequality gives ∥G∥≤1\|G\|\le1∥G∥≤1. Since 1∗=11^*=11∗=1 and F(1)=1F(1)=1F(1)=1,

G(1)=12[1+1‾]=1.G(1)=\tfrac12[1+\overline1]=1.G(1)=21​[1+1]=1.

Evaluation at the norm-one identity gives 1=∣G(1)∣≤∥G∥1=|G(1)|\le\|G\|1=∣G(1)∣≤∥G∥, proving equality. Finally (F∗)∗=F(F^*)^*=F(F∗)∗=F, and conjugate linearity of the functional adjoint on scalar coefficients gives G∗=GG^*=GG∗=G. Exercise 4. The directional formula (4) must hold for an arbitrary, possibly nonseparable, unital Banach algebra CCC. For a∈Ca\in Ca∈C, put q(s)=(∥1+sa∥−1)/sq(s)=(\|1+sa\|-1)/sq(s)=(∥1+sa∥−1)/s. Explain how compactness of the entire dual unit ball supplies the limiting normalized functional, and how its subnet preserves the scalar limsup. Also identify why a convergent functional subsequence cannot be assumed.

Solution. Section 9 uses one disk of radius ∥x∥\|x\|∥x∥ for every x∈Cx\in Cx∈C. In their product, impose all equations f(x+λy)=f(x)+λf(y)f(x+\lambda y)=f(x)+\lambda f(y)f(x+λy)=f(x)+λf(y). Each equation is closed in the coordinate topology. Their intersection consists exactly of linear functionals of norm at most one, so it is the weak-* dual ball. The ultrafilter proof of product compactness works for the full index set CCC; it imposes no countability condition.

The triangle inequality gives ∣q(s)∣≤∥a∥|q(s)|\le\|a\|∣q(s)∣≤∥a∥, so its scalar limsup LLL is finite. Choose a strictly decreasing sequence sn↓0s_n\downarrow0sn​↓0 with q(sn)→Lq(s_n)\to Lq(sn​)→L, by taking sns_nsn​ below the previous half-step and below a threshold on which q<L+1/nq<L+1/nq<L+1/n, while ensuring q(sn)>L−1/nq(s_n)>L-1/nq(sn​)>L−1/n. For all sufficiently large nnn, 1+sna≠01+s_na\ne01+sn​a=0. Section 8.1 supplies ∥Fn∥=1\|F_n\|=1∥Fn​∥=1 with Fn(1+sna)=∥1+sna∥F_n(1+s_na)=\|1+s_na\|Fn​(1+sn​a)=∥1+sn​a∥.

Compactness gives a cluster point FFF in the full dual ball. More explicitly, intersect the closures of all tails of (Fn)(F_n)(Fn​). They have the finite intersection property, so that intersection is nonempty. The inequalities apply to differences of real tensors. 8. Norm-preserving functional extension

We use extension in three places: to norm a vector in the projective algebra, to extend a limit on span⁡C{1,a}\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{1,a\}spanC​{1,a}, and to extend a spectral evaluation to a state. The construction below works on arbitrary subspaces of arbitrary normed spaces, whether or not they are closed or complete.

8.1. The precise norming-functional input

For t=−b<0t=-b<0t=−b<0, the lower inequality at y/by/by/b gives g(y)−bc≤p(y−bz)g(y)-bc\le p(y-bz)g(y)−bc≤p(y−bz). Partially order all such extensions by extension of both domain and functional. In a chain, the union of the domains is a vector subspace: any two vectors lie together in one of the comparable domains. 9. Weak-star compactness for arbitrary normed spaces

This supplies compactness of the state spaces and the alternative Banach–Alaoglu argument in Exercise 4. The closed unit dual ball is compact in the weak-star topology for every real or complex normed space; separability and completeness of the original space are unnecessary. The foundation boundary is ZFC, including Zorn’s lemma, scalar completeness and topology, and the definitions of a norm, a product topology and a weak-star topology. The needed arbitrary product step is proved here.

9.1. Proper filters and maximal extensions

A proper filter on a nonempty set SSS is a family of subsets containing SSS, excluding the empty set, closed under finite intersections and upward inclusion. A family with the finite intersection property generates a proper filter by taking all supersets of its finite intersections. Order proper filters extending a fixed proper filter by inclusion. For a nonempty chain of proper filters extending the fixed filter, their union again contains the fixed filter and excludes the empty set. Any finite list of members of the union lies in a single filter of the chain: choose a filter containing each member and use the total ordering by inclusion to take the largest of the finitely many selected filters. Their intersection therefore belongs to the union and is nonempty. Upward closure also passes to the union. The fixed filter itself is an upper bound for the empty chain. Thus every chain has an upper bound in the ordered family, and Zorn's lemma gives a maximal proper extension. The maximal extension is denoted U\mathcal UU.

For any A⊂SA\subset SA⊂S, either A∈UA\in\mathcal UA∈U or S∖A∈US\setminus A\in\mathcal US∖A∈U. Indeed, if adjoining AAA produced a proper filter, maximality would put AAA in U\mathcal UU. Otherwise some F∈UF\in\mathcal UF∈U has F∩A=∅F\cap A=\varnothingF∩A=∅, so F⊂S∖AF\subset S\setminus AF⊂S∖A, and upward inclusion puts the complement in U\mathcal UU. Such a maximal filter is an ultrafilter. If finitely many subsets cover a member of U\mathcal UU, one of them is in U\mathcal UU: otherwise all their complements would be in it, contradicting the nonempty-intersection requirement.

9.2. Every ultrafilter on a closed scalar disk converges

Let Dr={z∈C:∣z∣≤r}D_r=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|\le r\}Dr​={z∈C:∣z∣≤r}, where r≥0r\ge0r≥0, and let U\mathcal UU be an ultrafilter on DrD_rDr​. For r=0r=0r=0, the disk is a singleton. For r>0r>0r>0, begin with the closed square [−r,r]2[-r,r]^2[−r,r]2 and divide both coordinate intervals into halves. Its four closed subsquares cover the disk, so the preceding finite-cover argument selects a subsquare Q1Q_1Q1​ for which Dr∩Q1∈UD_r\cap Q_1\in\mathcal UDr​∩Q1​∈U. Continue within that square. This gives nested closed squares QnQ_nQn​, with Dr∩Qn∈UD_r\cap Q_n\in\mathcal UDr​∩Qn​∈U, and diameters tending to zero.

Write either coordinate interval of QnQ_nQn​ as [an,bn][a_n,b_n][an​,bn​]. The left endpoints increase, the right endpoints decrease, and bn−an→0b_n-a_n\to0bn​−an​→0. By real completeness, c=sup⁡nanc=\sup_n a_nc=supn​an​ exists. Nestedness gives an≤c≤bna_n\le c\le b_nan​≤c≤bn​ for every nnn; the vanishing lengths make ccc the only point in every interval. Applying this to both coordinates gives a unique point zzz in every square. The proper-filter condition makes every Dr∩QnD_r\cap Q_nDr​∩Qn​ nonempty. Choose wnw_nwn​ there; then ∣wn−z∣≤diam⁡(Qn)→0|w_n-z|\le\operatorname{diam}(Q_n)\to0∣wn​−z∣≤diam(Qn​)→0, so the reverse triangle inequality gives ∣z∣≤r|z|\le r∣z∣≤r. Every disk neighborhood of zzz contains Dr∩QnD_r\cap Q_nDr​∩Qn​ for all sufficiently large nnn, hence belongs to the ultrafilter. This proves convergence. In the real case there is only one coordinate interval.

9.3. Arbitrary products of these disks are compact

Let P=∏i∈IDriP=\prod_{i\in I}D_{r_i}P=∏i∈I​Dri​​, with its product topology; the point whose every coordinate is zero shows P≠∅P\ne\varnothingP=∅. If U\mathcal UU is an ultrafilter on PPP, its image under a coordinate projection is an ultrafilter on the corresponding disk: a subset belongs to that image filter precisely when its inverse image belongs to U\mathcal UU. The filter and complement rules pass through inverse images. Each image ultrafilter converges to a coordinate ziz_izi​. These coordinates define z∈Pz\in Pz∈P.

A basic neighborhood of zzz restricts only finitely many coordinates. Each inverse image of a restricted-coordinate neighborhood belongs to U\mathcal UU; their finite intersection does as well. Every neighborhood contains such a basic neighborhood, so U\mathcal UU converges to zzz.

Now suppose an open cover of PPP had no finite subcover. The complements of its members would have the finite intersection property. Extend their generated proper filter to an ultrafilter and let it converge to zzz. A cover member containing zzz is a neighborhood and therefore belongs to the ultrafilter. Its complement belongs to it by construction, a contradiction. Thus every open cover has a finite subcover. This proves the precise arbitrary-product compactness needed here.

9.4. The dual ball is a closed subspace of the product

Let XXX be a complex normed space and set

PX=∏x∈X{z∈C:∣z∣≤∥x∥}.P_X=\prod_{x\in X}\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|\le\|x\|\}.PX​=x∈X∏​{z∈C:∣z∣≤∥x∥}.

An element b∈PXb\in P_Xb∈PX​ is a scalar-valued function on XXX with ∣b(x)∣≤∥x∥|b(x)|\le\|x\|∣b(x)∣≤∥x∥. For each x,y∈Xx,y\in Xx,y∈X and λ∈C\lambda\in\mathbb Cλ∈C, the function

b⟼b(x+λy)−b(x)−λb(y)b\longmapsto b(x+\lambda y)-b(x)-\lambda b(y)b⟼b(x+λy)−b(x)−λb(y)

is continuous, since coordinate evaluations and finite scalar linear combinations are continuous. Its zero set is closed. Intersect all these zero sets. The intersection consists exactly of complex-linear functions satisfying the displayed bound: taking x=y=0x=y=0x=y=0 first gives b(0)=0b(0)=0b(0)=0, and the equations then give additivity and homogeneity. Such a function is continuous, because ∣b(x)−b(y)∣≤∥x−y∥|b(x)-b(y)|\le\|x-y\|∣b(x)−b(y)∣≤∥x−y∥, and has functional norm at most one. Conversely every functional of norm at most one belongs to this intersection.

Thus the closed unit ball of X∗X^*X∗ is a closed subset of the compact space PXP_XPX​. A closed subset of a compact space is compact: extend any relative open cover to an ambient open cover by adding its open complement, take a finite subcover, then discard the complement. The restricted product topology is exactly the weak-star topology, because both are the topology generated by the evaluations f↦f(x)f\mapsto f(x)f↦f(x). This proves the required compactness. For real XXX, use real intervals and real coefficients.

The limiting functional argument and the two-dimensional restriction argument prove the same directional formula. Section 8.3 combines this arbitrary dual-ball compactness with the closed positivity conditions needed for the common-state selection.
